title: 302 redirects with Cache-Control: no-store
context: Issue recommends starting with 302; disabled and expired links must stop working.
options: 301: browsers and proxies cache it, so a later disable or edit may never be seen
302 with default caching: some intermediaries may still cache briefly
302 plus no-store: every visit comes back to us
why: Following the issue's recommendation. no-store is what makes disabling and expiry take effect immediately; the cost is one indexed lookup per visit, which is the cheap path anyway.

title: Disabled and expired links return 410 Gone with distinct error codes
context: Issue asks for an appropriate error for disabled or expired links, separate from the 404 for unknown codes.
options: 404 for everything: hides that the link existed, but clients cannot tell why it fails
403 for disabled: implies an auth problem the user could fix
why: 410 says the link existed and is permanently unusable, which is accurate for both cases. The responses use the same JSON error envelope as the API, not an HTML page.

anchors.snippet: return error_response(410, "link_disabled", "this short link has been disabled")

title: Keep redirects to one indexed SELECT, and reject impossible codes before touching the database
context: Issue asks to avoid unnecessary database operations and optimize redirect performance.
options: Add an in-process cache of code to URL: fewer queries, but disabling would need cache invalidation across workers
Count clicks on redirect: useful stats, but a write on every visit
One SELECT on the unique index, no writes, and a regex check that turns favicon.ico and other impossible codes into a 404 with no connection opened
choice: Single indexed SELECT, no writes, regex fast-path
why: An indexed SQLite lookup with WAL is already sub-millisecond, so a cache adds invalidation bugs for little gain. A test traces the SQL to show exactly one SELECT per redirect. Click counting is left for a later issue.

title: Send the stored URL verbatim as Location, only percent-encoding non-ASCII characters
context: Acceptance criteria require the destination path and query parameters be preserved.
options: Let Werkzeug's redirect() build the header: it writes non-ASCII bytes raw, which breaks the header
Re-parse and rebuild the URL: risks normalizing away meaningful escapes like %2F
iri_to_uri on the stored string: keeps existing escapes and ordering, encodes only what must be encoded
choice: iri_to_uri on the stored URL; the request's own query string is not appended
why: Tests check that paths, repeated and empty query parameters, escaped values and fragments come back byte-for-byte. Appending the request's own query string to the destination is a feature some shorteners have, but nothing here asked for it.
